title: The Global War On VPNs Draws Closer

content_html:
from the the-war-on-your-privacy-and-security dept

Back in March, Walled Culture noted that companies were increasing their attacks on VPNs, in part because of claims that the latter were being widely used for the circumvention of copyright law. Unfortunately, since then the trend discussed there has continued, with a notable uptick in recent months. For example, the LaLiga professional association football league in Spain, which has appeared a number of times on this blog, has called for major VPNs to be placed on the European Union’s “Counterfeit and Piracy Watch List”. TorrentFreak explains:

The 14-page submission targets a wide range of sites and services, including traditional piracy threats, but the VPN section is new. The league notes that it doesn’t take offense with the technology itself, but with how these providers are marketed by others through their affiliate programs.

That may be so, but putting VPN providers on “counterfeit and piracy watch lists” is a slippery slope. Once the precedent is established, it will be easy for others to claim that the marketing of a VPN provider is somehow promoting copyright infringement. And once VPNs are officially associated with breaking the law in this way, it will be natural to attack them more vigorously.

That is what is beginning to happen in the US, with a number of legislative proposals that would impact VPNs. For example, the absurdly named “Shielding Children’s Retinas from Egregious Exposure on the Net Act” or the “SCREEN Act”. The EFF explains that the main aim of the bill is to require online services to verify users’ ages before they can access any sexually explicit content. But VPNs are explicitly targeted:

The bill requires covered websites to verify users’ ages based on their IP addresses unless the service can determine that the user is outside the United States, and specifically requires age verification on traffic coming from known VPN addresses. In practice, this discourages the use of VPNs and proxy servers, which millions of people rely on for legitimate purposes such as protecting personal privacy, securing public Wi-Fi connections, safeguarding journalists and activists, and preventing data tracking.

TorrentFreak has news about another US bill, the American Copyright Protection Act (ACPA), which also targets VPNs:

Under the ACPA, any broadband provider, DNS resolver, or VPN with 100,000 or more monthly users or subscribers in the United States can be named in a blocking order. Smaller services are exempt, as well as root nameservers and top-level domain registries.

Interestingly, a “competing” site-blocking proposal is notable for not including VPNs in its scope:

The DEFEND IP Act explicitly excludes services that exclusively provide VPN connections or similar encrypted routing, as well as DNS services that only work through encrypted protocols, such as DoH.

That’s welcome, but it’s not yet clear which of those differing approaches, if any, will become law. Meanwhile, it is only too clear that VPNs are already under attack. This has prompted some pushback from the Internet Infrastructure Coalition:

The i2Coalition (Internet Infrastructure Coalition) ensures that those who build the infrastructure of the Internet have a voice in public policy. We are the leading voice for web hosting companies, data centers, domain registrars and registries, cloud infrastructure providers, managed services providers, and related tech. We protect innovation and the continued growth of the Internet’s infrastructure, which are essential to the global economy.

It has a site called VPNs at Risk, and a new report of the same name, which it says is “A comprehensive, content-neutral look at the technical and human impact of proposals affecting Virtual Private Networks.” It is a good introduction to the entire field, providing an approachable explanation of the technology that lies behind VPNs, as well as a useful survey of VPN regulations around the world, including those in India, United Kingdom, Pakistan, France, Iran, and Russia. It points out that there is a need for a broader conversation, since the questions raised by VPNs are not unique to that field:

Similar debates increasingly surround encryption, cloud computing, hosting, domain name systems, artificial intelligence, digital identity, and other technologies that provide general-purpose capabilities upon which many different users and services depend.

The rapid development and adoption of artificial intelligence make this broader conversation more urgent. As more consequential activities depend on connected systems, strong encryption, secure networking, and trustworthy Internet infrastructure become increasingly important. Policies that weaken these foundations can create vulnerabilities that extend well beyond their immediate targets. Addressing emerging risks should strengthen the infrastructure on which people and organizations depend, rather than compromise the tools that protect it.

An article on the Disruptive Competition Project (DisCo) site, which comes from the Computer & Communication Industry Association (CCIA), discusses a proposal currently being considered by the European Commission:

an EU-wide system of anti-piracy injunctions – requiring providers to block access to websites and servers containing copyright-infringing content. Such a system risks turning providers of virtual private networks (VPNs) into watchdogs that have to filter traffic, undermining their core privacy-protecting function.

The DisCo article makes an important point:

In practice, pirates can quickly circumvent such measures, meaning that injunctions harm users’ privacy without delivering lasting results. Yet the blocking system remains under consideration for the Commission’s Copyright Package, due in the second quarter of 2027.

Instead, it suggests:

It’s time for EU policy- and decision-makers to commit unequivocally to preserving strong privacy protections and encryption, to focus anti-piracy enforcement on services that host illegal content and also have the ability to remove it, and to maintain a predictable regulatory environment for trusted VPN providers.

That certainly makes sense, but sense has never been much in evidence in the copyright world, which is driven by emotion and lobbying. Instead, we can probably expect increasingly strident calls for VPNs to be “reined in” in order to protect copyright – and the children, of course…
